title: Carmen’s liberty
where: *Carmen*, Act 1, Scene 5; Act 2, Scenes 5 and 6; Act 3, Scene 2 (the scene numbers of the French libretto)
about: In a square in Seville the young men ask Carmen, a gypsy, when she will love them. She answers with a song, then throws a flower at the one man still at his work, the soldier Don José. He goes to prison for her, and the night he comes out she says that if he loved her he would follow her to the mountains; he refuses, then draws his sword on an officer and has to go. In Act 3, among smugglers, she turns up death in the cards.

view.says: In *The Enchafèd Flood* Auden describes the wilderness of the Romantics, sea or desert, as the place with no community, where a person is free alike of the evils and of the duties of life among others. Byron’s ocean is one example, Captain Nemo’s sea another, and Carmen’s mountains a third. Such places are marked by the absence of limits. Because they are free, he adds, they are lonely.
view.quote: And so Carmen tempts Don José to leave the fertile plain for the barren lawless mountains.
view.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), pp. 15–17
view.checked: read in the scan of The Enchafèd Flood, research/auden/ef.txt lines 676-790, on 2026-10-03, by the poet before me and again by me. In this scan the page number stands at the foot: the no-community sentences are on p. 15, the Carmen sentence with four quoted lines and the absence of limitations on p. 16, six more lines, the credit to Meilhac and Halévy and the lonely places on p. 17. The scan prints Jose without its accent. Second examiner, 2026-10-03: read again in the same scan, whose title page gives the Vintage Books edition of September 1967, so the page numbers are that edition’s; the quotation was compared with the scan by script, letter for letter apart from the accent, and matched.

points.say: The line ends on a mute *e*. The count leaves it out. In singing, the same history of French verse says, it is always sounded in full.
A vowel follows, so this final *e* is not counted.
A consonant follows, so this final *e* is a syllable.
One word, printed twice: as printed, the line has ten syllables. After the second verse the refrain is printed again with the word once, and there this line has eight.

lenses.caption: French verse is measured by the number of syllables. Here the line has eight, which a history of French verse gives as the line of lyric pieces and lighter poetry: Carmen is answering the young men with a song. The endings go by turns: a mute e, which the count leaves out and a singer sounds, then a full syllable. One line of the refrain is printed with a word twice, and has ten. Auden says a libretto’s verses are addressed to the composer. By Winton Dean’s account the composer wrote these himself, and the tune is adapted from a song by Sebastián Yradier with the same plan, verse in the minor and refrain in the major.
lenses.why: Carmen answers the young men in the eight-syllable line of lyric and lighter verse; the line printed with ten has a word twice; the verses, which Auden says are addressed to the composer, were by Dean’s account the composer’s own.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: Littré’s first sense is one who rises against a lawful authority. His third belongs to the language of gallantry: one who does not yield to love.
Littré: to make tame, as a lion or birds. Familiarly, of a woman: to get her used to hearing love talked of.
One of Littré’s senses is a native of a place: the children of Paris.
Littré: gypsies are called *bohèmes* because they were thought to come from Bohemia. They are wandering bands with no fixed home and no regular trade, who often tell fortunes.
notes.source: Littré, under bohème, 1 and the etymology

notes.note: Littré’s first sense is a rule laid down by the sovereign authority. His seventeenth is the sway a woman has over a man.
Littré: with the verb *to take*, to watch out, to take one’s precautions.

lenses.caption: In Littré’s dictionary three of these words have a sense in the language of courtship. Rebelle is one who will not yield to love. Apprivoiser, to tame, is to get a woman used to hearing love talked of. Loi, law, is the sway a woman has over a man. The song turns all three on love itself, in their first senses: love is the rebel against authority, the bird not to be tamed, the one that knows no law. The refrain gives it a country, Bohême, Bohemia, where gypsies were thought to come from, and Carmen is a gypsy. Auden names Carmen as the classic case of a type of woman, the Infernal Venus, who is against all order.
lenses.why: The song gives three words of courtship, rebel, tame and law, in their first senses to love itself, and makes love a gypsy like the singer; Auden names Carmen the classic case of the woman against all order.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: anadiplosis
lenses.plain: a doubling back: the words that end one clause begin the next; here they come back after a second *si*
lenses.caption: The refrain ends on two sentences built alike: si, if, a condition, then a result. Both conditions are in the present; in Act 2 she will say what would happen if. The result of the first, that she loves, comes back after the second si as its condition, the link rhetoric calls anadiplosis, and from it follows a warning. So the warning is for the one who does not love her. The pronoun is tu, one person, though many men asked. One man, José, has gone on working; after the song she goes straight to him, and left alone he puts it down to his paying her no attention. Auden’s example of a lifelong one-sided romance is José and Carmen.
lenses.why: The result of the first if-sentence is the condition of the second, so the warning falls on whoever does not love her, on stage José, the one man at his work; Auden’s example of a one-sided romance is these two.

grounds.claim: the two ifs; the pronoun and verb that end the first sentence stand again after the second if; the one spoken to is the subject of the verb to love once, with a negation; the pronoun for the one spoken to is the singular; the verbs are in the present and the last is an imperative
anadiplosis: the repetition of the last word or phrase of one line, clause or sentence at the beginning of the next
grounds.source: Silva Rhetoricae (rhetoric.byu.edu), under anadiplosis, read in the saved page on 2026-10-03

grounds.claim: a conditional sentence has a condition introduced by si and a result; a result in the present indicative, the imperative or the future requires the if-clause in the present indicative, and a result in the conditional requires it in the imperfect; the conditional says what would happen in case something else were to happen
grounds.source: W. H. Fraser and J. Squair, High School French Grammar (Toronto, 1900), sections 265, 274 and 275

grounds.claim: in Act 2 her if-clause is in the imperfect and its result in the conditional

lenses.label: English

ties.say: *To tame* is kept, and kept at the end of the line, where the English rhymes it two lines on.
The French gives love a birthplace, Bohemia, and so makes it a gypsy. The English gives it a rank: a *lord*.
The French word stands twice, and the line as printed has ten syllables. The English line has ten as well; this adjective is one of the words it adds.
The French has one bare noun, *loi*, law. The English gives the law *fetters*.
Both *ifs* are kept, and the present tense with them.
Four French words of warning, one English word. It rhymes with the last word two lines up.

lenses.caption: This English seems made for singing. It rhymes every second line, and its first four lines count nine, eight, nine and eight syllables, as the French lines do when the mute e is sung. The line the French prints with ten has ten here. What is named changes. The French gives love a birthplace, Bohême, Bohemia, the gypsies’ supposed home; the English gives it a rank, a lord. For the bare noun loi, law, the English has fetters, to be worn, and that verb is its rhyme. Auden was not, as a rule, for opera in translation: a composer, he held, writes for the syllables.
lenses.why: The English keeps the sung count in its first lines and a rhyme, and changes what is named: the gypsy with no law becomes a lord who will wear no fetters; Auden held that a composer writes for the syllables.

the first four English lines have nine, eight, nine and eight syllables; the second line of the English refrain has eight words and ten syllables, the third nine, the fourth eight; that second line has a negative, the law in the possessive, an adjective, fetters, and ends on the verb to wear; by the second examiner’s count rows 6 and 9 of the block have eight syllables where the French line as sung has nine, so the caption claims the count only for the first four lines and the line of ten

lenses.label: Mood
lenses.caption: The first sentence is a supposition. After si, if, the verb is in the imperfect, aimais, loved, and the result in the conditional, suivrais, would follow: the form, a French grammar says, for what would happen if. José has just sung what her flower was to him in prison, and she has answered that he does not love her. Later, where the stage direction calls him almost won over, she sings the line again with one letter gone: suivras, will follow. The if is gone too, and loved is now aimes, love. Auden’s verb for what she does to José is tempts.
lenses.why: Carmen first puts José’s following her as a supposition, if with the imperfect and the conditional; when he is almost won over she repeats the line in the future with no if; Auden’s verb for what she does is tempts.

grounds.claim: the if, the tense of each of the five verbs, and the one letter between the conditional and the future of the same verb

the stem of the conditional is that of the future; a result in the conditional has its if-clause in the imperfect and says what would happen in case something else were to happen; a result in the future has its if-clause in the present
grounds.source: W. H. Fraser and J. Squair, High School French Grammar (Toronto, 1900), sections 115 (observation), 116, 265 (1) and 275

grounds.claim: si is the conjunction of a condition or a supposition
grounds.source: Émile Littré, Dictionnaire de la langue française (1873–74), under si (1)

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. W. H. Fraser and J. Squair, *High School French Grammar* (1900), sections 115, 116, 265 and 275, for the conditional and the sentences it goes in. José’s song and her answer to it are in [Act 2](#/read/carmen/act-2:242); the direction that he is almost won over is in the French text only. Auden’s sentence: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 16.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: Littré: below, or at some distance. In these lines the place has no other name.
Set before a noun, *point* denies it, and the verb is left understood.
Littré: the duty of soldiers to be back at a set hour, and the signal given for it.
Littré: to lead a wandering life is to live at random, without aim.
Littré’s first sense is the unlimited system of the planets and stars. His third is the earth, or a great part of it.
Littré’s first sense: a rule laid down by the sovereign authority.
Littré: the power within by which a person decides to do or not to do.
Littré’s first sense is what makes drunk. The second is figurative: what deludes, exalts, charms.
Littré’s first sense: the condition of a person who belongs to no master.

lenses.caption: In these lines the place has one name, là-bas, over there, said six times. It is described first by what it lacks: point, no, officer to obey, and no retraite, the bugle call back to barracks. José named that call when the bugles sounded and he said he must go. What it has comes in the last four lines, sung by all as the act ends, and Littré defines two of their words by a lack too: errante, not fixed, and liberté, having no master. Auden says such places are marked by the absence of limits. The thing prized above all is enivrante, intoxicating: in Littré what makes drunk and, by a figure, what deludes, exalts or charms.
lenses.why: In these lines the place is only over there, described by what it lacks, no officer and no call to barracks, and by words Littré defines as lacks; Auden marks such places by the absence of limits.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: isocolon
lenses.plain: parts of the same length and the same build, set side by side
lenses.caption: The last four lines have no verb. Each of the first two is cut into matched halves: the open sky, the wandering life; then for country the whole world, for law one’s own will. In the long line each half has six syllables: pour, for, a noun, then what stands in its place. In Littré loi is first a rule laid down by the sovereign authority: here that authority is oneself. The line rhymes volonté, will, with liberté. Auden quoted these four lines in 1943 as the song of a teacher who promises that nothing will be required: for the pupils, he said, the affair begins as Hans Andersen and ends as Grimm.
lenses.why: The list has no verb; its long line is two matched halves, each putting the whole world or one’s own will in place of a country or a law; Auden, quoting the lines, said the affair ends as Grimm.

grounds.claim: the two halves of each of the two lines; no verb in the last four lines; the last words of the second and fourth of them end alike

lenses.label: English

ties.say: The French says *you would follow me*. The English says *would we go*, and adds *together*.
*Retraite* is the call back to barracks at a set hour. The English says only *the trumpet*.
The French now states it: *you love me*. The English keeps an *if*.
*For country, the whole world*. The English has *the wide world*, and makes it *our dwelling*.
*Sa volonté* is one’s own will, each person’s. The English says *our will*.
*Enivrante*, intoxicating, has no word in the English, which says that liberty surpasses the rest.

lenses.caption: Here the English does not rhyme and keeps to the order of the French. Three of its changes run one way. Tu me suivrais is you would follow me; the English has would we go, and adds together. Sa volonté is one’s own will; the English has our will, and our dwelling in the line before. In the French one person follows another, and the only law is each person’s will. Auden counts her mountains among the wild places with no community, and says that because such places are free they are lonely. The stage direction that opens the next act sets it in complete solitude and dark night.
lenses.why: Where the French has one person following another and each one’s own will for law, the English makes a we with our will; Auden counts her mountains among places with no community, free and for that reason lonely.

grounds.claim: which French words answer which English words

the French verb is you would follow me, and its possessive in the long line is the third person singular; the English has we, together and our; the English lines do not rhyme; no word for we, our or together stands in the French of these lines or of the speeches they are taken from

grounds.source: Émile Littré, Dictionnaire de la langue française (1873–74), under retraite (3), enivrant (1 and 2), univers (3) and volonté (1)

points.say: The cut. The sixth syllable ends a word and takes an accent, and the voice rests here.
Twelve syllables, then six, rhymed by turns. A history of French verse gives as its example of this stanza Malherbe’s poem consoling a friend on the death of his daughter.
The final *e* of *carte*, card, is a syllable here, because a consonant follows.
The same word. Here a vowel follows, and its *e* is not counted.
Eight syllables. The stanzas of twelve and six are over.

lenses.caption: French verse is measured by the number of syllables. A final e counts before a consonant, is dropped before a vowel, and is left out at a line’s end. The two women beside Carmen have just told their fortunes in lines of eight, with one line of ten in their refrain. Eight is the measure of her first song and, by a history of French verse, of lyric pieces and lighter poetry. Carmen has read death in four lines of her own. What she sings next is in another measure: a line of twelve, resting after its sixth syllable, then a line of six. The line of twelve has been the standard line of French tragedy since the sixteenth century.
lenses.why: The two women read their fortunes in the short line of song; when Carmen has read death in hers the verse changes to the line of twelve, which has been the standard line of French tragedy since the sixteenth century.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: Each stanza is four lines, rhymed by turns. Its long lines end on a syllable with a mute e, the ending French verse calls feminine: amères, bitter, sincères, sincere. Its short lines end on a full syllable, the masculine ending. French poets have alternated the two since the sixteenth century, and Ronsard gave the reason: verse so made is fitter for music. In singing, the mute e is heard like any other vowel. In the third stanza the short lines end on sort, fate, and mort, death. The last two lines rhyme as a pair: qu’importe, what does it matter, and forte, strong. Their rhyme keeps the sound or of sort and mort.
lenses.why: The stanzas keep the alternation of endings that Ronsard recommended to fit verse for music; the short lines of the third stanza end on the words for fate and death, and the couplet after it rhymes on their sound.

grounds.claim: which lines rhyme and on which letters: first with third and second with fourth in each of three sets of four lines (rows 0.0-0.3, 0.4-0.7 and 1.0-1.3), then the last two lines as a pair, so each of the three stanzas is four lines; which endings have a mute e; the letters or in five words, in four of the last five lines (rows 1.1, 1.3, 1.4 and 1.5)

Ronsard recommended alternating masculine and feminine lines so that verse would be fitter for music; poets have kept the rule since; in song the mute e of a feminine ending is audible like any other vowel
grounds.source: L. E. Kastner, A History of French Versification (Oxford, 1903), pp. 64–65, and p. 7, note 1

grounds.claim: sort is fate; mort is death; qu’importe expresses indifference; fort is strong; amer is bitter to the taste and, by a figure, painful; sincère is said of one who tells truly what he feels and thinks, and of things too
grounds.source: Émile Littré, Dictionnaire de la langue française (1873–74), under sort (1), mort (the noun, 1), importer (the second entry, 4), fort (1 and 18), amer (1 and 2) and sincère (1 and 2); the last two opened by the second examiner in the first examiner’s saved pages

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. L. E. Kastner, *A History of French Versification*, pp. 64–65, for the alternation of the two endings, Ronsard’s reason for it, and the mute *e* in singing. Littré under *amer*, *sincère*, *sort*, *mort*, *importer* and *fort*.

lenses.label: Build
lenses.caption: The second and third stanzas, marked here, are built alike: si, if, then a command, then what the card will do. If your page is lucky, shuffle and cut without fear. But if you must die, begin again twenty times. They differ at the line ends. In the second stanza the card and its verb share a line. In the third, each long line ends on its subject, the dread word, the pitiless card, and the verb waits for the short line. French classical critics, a history of French verse reports, held that a run-over hurries the reader past the rhyme into the next line, where a stronger pause then falls. Here it falls after sort, fate, and mort, death.
lenses.why: In the lucky stanza the card and its verb share a line; in the stanza of death both long lines break between subject and verb, so the voice runs past the rhyme and pauses after fate and death.

grounds.claim: where the three ifs, the two commands and each subject and verb stand; that the long lines of the third stanza end on a subject with no verb yet; that all eleven marks of this tab stand in the second and third stanzas (rows 0.4 to 0.6 and 1.0 to 1.3), and none in the first stanza, in row 0.7 or in the last two lines

what the two sentences say: if the page is lucky, shuffle and cut without fear, and the card will turn up joyful; but if you must die, if fate has written the dread word, begin again twenty times, and the pitiless card will always say death

a run-over carries a clause begun in one line into the next (p. 107); the classical poets allowed it when the part that runs over makes up all of the following line (p. 112), as it does here; their case against it, which Kastner reports and thinks well founded on the whole though pressed too far, was that words joined in grammar are not parted in reading, so that the reader passes quickly over the rhyme and a stronger pause falls in the next line (pp. 113–14)
grounds.source: L. E. Kastner, A History of French Versification (Oxford, 1903), pp. 107 and 112–14, read by the second examiner in the first examiner’s saved copy

grounds.claim: si is the conjunction of a condition; heureux is first that promises good luck; redoutable is to be dreaded; impitoyable is without pity; sort is fate; mort is death
grounds.source: Émile Littré, Dictionnaire de la langue française (1873–74), under si (1), heureux (1), redoutable, impitoyable (1), sort (1) and mort (the noun, 1)

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and what its two sentences say. L. E. Kastner, *A History of French Versification*, p. 107 for the run-over and pp. 113–14 for the classical case against it, which he reports. Littré under *si*, *heureux*, *redoutable*, *impitoyable*, *sort* and *mort*.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: The French says *tu*, you, in every stanza. The English says *I* in this one line, and *thou*, *thy* and *thee* after it.
*Mêler* and *couper* are the card player’s words: to shuffle the pack, then to cut it in two. The English says *throw* and *play*.

*Sort* is fate. In Littré it is also, among the ancients, a supposed way of learning the future by throwing dice, and the Latin word meant at first tallies of wood thrown on the ground. The English says *heaven*.
The French is a command: *begin again twenty times*. In its place the English has a clause that gives the cards a will.
The French sentence ends on the card’s own words, set in quotation marks: *la mort*, death. The English says *thy doom* here, and *death* in the line she sings next.
*Braver* is to face a person or a thing as a brave man does: to defy.
*La plus forte* is the strongest. The English says *strong*.

lenses.caption: The English is from a libretto sold in New York about 1910. It follows the French line by line, without the rhyme or the count. The French says tu, you, in every stanza; the English begins with I. Sort, fate, becomes heaven. The card’s own words, la mort, death, become thy doom. La plus forte, the strongest, becomes strong. In a lecture on Richard III, pieced together from listeners’ notes, Auden said that people of very strong will are inclined to a belief in fate and in signs, and his example was Carmen reading the cards. Both are in the French: what fate has written the card will say, and Carmen is the strongest.
lenses.why: Auden’s example of a strong will that believes in fate and signs is this scene, and the French words say both; the English has heaven for fate, doom for death and strong for the strongest.

grounds.claim: sort: destiny, taken as the cause of what happens in a life (1); among the ancients a supposed way of knowing the future with dice that were thrown (7; drawing lots is sense 8, not used here); from Latin sortem, the sortes being at first, by Mommsen’s account, tallies of wood on a cord that were thrown on the ground (the etymology). mêler: to shuffle the cards. couper: to divide the pack in two after the shuffle. braver: to act the brave man toward someone or something, to defy. mort: the end of life. fort: who has much strength

auden.says: In a talk at Swarthmore College in January 1943 Auden sets the old schoolmaster, who flogged, against the progressive educator, whom he calls a Carmen wrapped in cellophane: one who sings of a land where nobody suffers and nothing is required of anyone, and there is only the self and its expression. He then quotes the four lines on liberty that close Act 2, and adds that this affair, as the little Don Josés soon find out, begins as Hans Andersen and ends as Grimm.
auden.source: “Vocation and Society” (1943), in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), p. 179
auden.checked: snippets of the scanned volume at archive.org (item prosetravelbooks0000aude), chained by me on 2026-10-03 and saved in the scratchpad (carmen-poet/fts_prosetravelbooks0000aude_*.json): the sentence on the two educators, the four lines of the libretto, and the sentence after them on Hans Andersen and Grimm; also the editor’s textual note, which says the essay was based on a talk to the Swarthmore chapter of Phi Beta Kappa on 15 January 1943. The page: the lecture begins on p. 175 (running head and textual note); the running head of p. 179 stands about 370 words before the sentence, and the next head the search text has is that of p. 181, about 580 words after the sentence on Grimm; no head for p. 180 is in the search text. The two pages hold about 1,000 words, so the passage (words 340 to 430 of them) is most probably all on p. 179. The same text was read earlier in snippets of Auden Studies 3 (item insolitudeforcom0000aude), where the poet took it to have been first printed, pp. 15-30. Not seen as a page. Examiners, 2026-10-03: the first examiner found the page in the search inside the volume at Google Books (Prose. 1939-1948, 2002), which gives the page with each hit: the sentence on the educator, the four lines and the sentence on Hans Andersen and Grimm are all on p. 179. auden.says: In his New York lecture on *Richard III*, as an editor has put it together from the notes of people who heard it, Auden says that the more a man masters other people’s wills, the more what he did not intend and cannot control comes to matter to him. He gives Carmen reading the cards as his example of the rule quoted here.
auden.quote: Very strong-willed people are apt to believe in fate and signs
auden.source: *Lectures on Shakespeare*, reconstructed and edited by Arthur Kirsch (2000), p. 21

The page itself was not seen.

auden.says: Writing of Tristan and of Don Giovanni, Auden says that to idolize one real person romantically for a whole life is possible, and does happen, on one condition: the love must be on one side only, with one of the two playing the Cruel Fair. His example is Don José and Carmen. An idol, he explains, is what a person makes answerable for his own existence, and it is an idol no longer once it makes a claim on him in return.
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 121
auden.checked: read again by the second examiner, lines 5792-5814 of the same scan, on 2026-10-03; first read in the scan of The Dyer’s Hand, research/auden/dh.txt lines 5808-5814, on 2026-10-03; the running head [ 121 stands at line 5776 and 122 ] at line 5820. Finisher, 2026-10-03: lines 5808-5814 read again. He calls the idolatry lifelong, names José before Carmen, and does not say which of the two plays the Cruel Fair. The Figure caption of the first passage now names the two in his order and has his word lifelong; it does not say which is which

auden.says: In a piece of 1947 on the mythical types of woman, Auden’s second type is the Infernal Venus. She lures men to ruin and is against order of every kind. She stirs men and leaves them unhappy, and as a rule she ends badly. Her classic case, he writes, is Carmen, and he follows the sentence with a passage of Mérimée’s story.
auden.source: “The Mythical Sex” (1947), in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), p. 328
auden.checked: snippets of the scanned volume at archive.org (item prosetravelbooks0000aude), chained by the poet before me (notes.md): the textual note gives the title and p. 325 for the start; the Carmen sentence is followed at once by the running head of p. 329, so it stands at the foot of p. 328. Not seen as a page.

auden.says: In a piece written for *Vogue* in 1948 Auden says that opera is about willed feeling: there could be none unless people, besides having emotions, insisted on having them, whatever trouble that gives themselves and others. Every great character of opera, he says, is of this kind, and Carmen is one of the six he names.

The textual note says the piece begins on p. 400; the page of this sentence was not seen (probably p. 401). auden.says: Of the words of an opera Auden says that the verses a librettist writes are addressed to the composer and not to the public, and that their work is done once they have given him a melody. In song, he holds, a listener hears syllables and not words, and it is the syllables that decide what vocal line a composer writes. For that reason he is not, as a rule, in favor of performing operas in translation.
auden.source: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 473
auden.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer’s Hand, research/auden/dh.txt lines 22240-22300, on 2026-10-03. Examiners, 2026-10-03: the head of p. 473 stands at line 22253 and that of p. 474 at line 22301, and everything reported here lies between them, so the page is 473 alone

auden.says: Donald Pearce, who took the course of 1941, remembers that when he asked to join it Auden told him there would be opera scores and libretti, and named *Carmen* first. That semester Auden lectured often on love, and the class was set the libretti of *Tristan und Isolde* and *Carmen*, with *Romeo and Juliet* and Denis de Rougemont’s *Love in the Western World*. On neither page does Pearce report anything Auden said of the opera itself.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 133 and 137
auden.checked: read in the scan of Pearce’s essay, research/auden/pearce.txt, on 2026-10-03. The research notes give p. 136 for the second; by the scan it is p. 137. Second examiner, 2026-10-03: both places read again in the scan, the foot number 133 just after the first; the entry now claims only what the two places report.

auden.says: By Alan Ansen’s record of his talk in the late 1940s, Auden thought *Carmen* a very great work.
auden.source: Alan Ansen, *The Table Talk of W. H. Auden*, edited by Nicholas Jenkins (1990), p. 18

caveats: The English is from a libretto sold in New York about 1910, with no translator named. In the first song it rhymes every second line and seems made for singing; in the other two passages it keeps the order of the French without rhyme. It is not a close translation.

Auden’s remark on Carmen and the cards comes from a lecture pieced together by an editor from listeners’ notes. It was read here only in snippets of a scanned copy, as were his pieces of 1943, 1947 and 1948, Ansen’s record of his talk and Winton Dean’s book on Bizet.

The marks show the count of syllables and the accents the rule fixes, on the sixth syllable of a long line and the last of every line. French verse leaves the other stresses free, and they are not marked.

The second passage sets together three places in Act 2: five lines of Carmen’s to José, two that she sings a little later, and four that everyone sings as the act ends. Auden quotes one line more of her speech than the French text printed here has.

The first passage is the first of the song’s two verses and its refrain; the French text prints the refrain’s second line with one word twice, then once; no score was consulted. By Winton Dean’s account its words are Bizet’s own, and he also reworked those of the card solo.
